identity.title: GPS Tracker Logger
identity.tagline: Live latitude, longitude, and speed, decoded from satellite signals and shown on a tiny screen.

goal: Read live position data from a NEO-6M GPS module and display latitude, longitude, and speed on an OLED — the same underlying technique behind dedicated GPS trackers and any project that needs to know where it physically is.
simpleSummary: Read your live location from a GPS module and show it on a small screen.
howItWorks: A GPS module doesn't calculate its own position from scratch — it listens to precisely-timed signals from multiple satellites simultaneously and calculates position from the tiny differences in when each signal arrives, then reports the result as a continuous stream of standardized text sentences (the NMEA format) over a plain serial connection. Those sentences are dense and not meant to be read directly (a typical one looks like a cryptic string of comma-separated numbers), which is why this project uses the TinyGPS++ library to parse them into plain latitude, longitude, and speed values. Because the GPS module needs its own serial connection separate from the Arduino's USB/programming serial port, this project uses SoftwareSerial to create a second, dedicated channel just for talking to it.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
Clear view of the sky (or a window) — GPS modules can take a minute or two to get their first fix
circuitDiagramCaption: GPS module on a SoftwareSerial pair (D3/D4); OLED on the I2C bus (A4/A5).

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the GPS module's TXD to Arduino D4, RXD to D3, VCC to 5V, and GND to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: As with any serial connection between two devices, this is crossed — the module's transmit pin goes to the pin the code treats as its receive pin.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the OLED's GND to GND, VCC to 5V, SDA to A4, and SCL to A5.
wiringSteps.detail: Same OLED wiring pattern used across every I2C-display project in this encyclopedia.

wiringSteps.instruction: Position the GPS module's antenna with a clear, unobstructed view of the sky — a window ledge works, a fully enclosed indoor room usually does not.
wiringSteps.detail: This is the step most likely to make the project seem broken when it isn't — see Troubleshooting for how long a first "cold start" fix realistically takes.

code.explanation: gps.encode() is fed one raw byte at a time from the module's serial stream, and internally accumulates those bytes into complete NMEA sentences, silently discarding anything malformed — this is why the read loop runs on every single pass rather than waiting for a whole line at once. gps.location.isUpdated() only returns true once a fresh, complete position sentence has actually been parsed, which avoids redrawing the OLED with the exact same numbers dozens of times per second between real updates.

expectedBehavior: Outdoors (or near a window) with a clear sky view, the OLED shows live latitude, longitude, speed, and the number of satellites currently in view, updating every time a new position sentence arrives — typically about once per second once a fix is established.

troubleshooting.issue: No data at all / satellite count stays at 0 for a long time.
troubleshooting.fix: A GPS module's very first "cold start" fix can genuinely take 30 seconds to a few minutes outdoors with clear sky view — this is normal satellite-almanac download behavior, not a fault. It won't get a fix at all fully indoors.
Same I2C address/wiring troubleshooting as every other OLED-based project in this encyclopedia.

troubleshooting.issue: Position updates but seems inaccurate by tens of meters.
troubleshooting.fix: This is normal for consumer-grade GPS modules like the NEO-6M — expect roughly 2.5-5 meter accuracy under good conditions, not survey-grade precision.

extensions: Log a full track (a list of lat/lng points over time) to an SD card instead of only showing the current position.
Add a geofence alert that triggers a buzzer if the tracked position leaves a defined area.
Combine with the Smart Home Sensor Hub's WiFi web server pattern to view live position from a phone browser instead of only the OLED.
Calculate and display distance traveled by summing the distance between consecutive fixes.
